doc.title: Sam Kininger interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, May 27, 2011

title: Rap, rhythmic phrasing and staccato melodies
summary: Sam loves rap; emphasizes rhythmic phrasing and short percussive lines.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Any kind of music that you don’t like? How would you know, you don’t listen to it, right?
I can say I don’t listen to country. I won’t say I don’t like it, but I mean like I said, I have a really broad range of styles, but I don’t listen to a lot of country I will say that.
Oh I love it, love it, yeah. Definitely a big influence also.
Yeah, yeah. And there’s two things I think of when I play it too are drums and the rapper’s passion. Like the way they flow, or the way their articulation on it.
Like hip hop, like rappers, emcees if you want to call it. Definitely rhythmic phrasing is what I definitely emphasize, more so than melodic.
Well I’ve noticed that some of the melodies I’ve heard you play are like staccato with a capital S [scats]. You know they’re very —

Yeah. Short. That’s what — me and Ryan joke about that too because you don’t really have to be in tune because we like play it so fast that it sounds in tune. Like [brief horn] ah the reed’s all dry, but you have to slow it down to really hear, was that in tune? But yeah. A lot of it is very percussive situations and fast.
